Draft text of the methods and their results, in three parts generated from outputs/data/ (the numbers are locked by tests/test_regression_model_v1.py). The figures of the paper: outputs/headline/HEADLINE.md; every other figure: outputs/diagnostics/DIAGNOSTICS.md; every output file: outputs/INDEX.md.

## 1. Baseline projection

Every result below is read from the run outputs (outputs/data/; settings from projection.py). Adopted run: Reference (net replacement half-life 10 yr); 2026 overbuild rule `market_excess`.

### Summary

New Zealand is projected to build 89.6 million m² of new residential floor area in 2026–2050 in the Reference. In 2026–2050 this emits 21.6 Mt CO₂e: 21.2 Mt from materials and construction (A1–A5) and soil carbon loss, counted in the construction year, and 403 kt of maintenance (B2, B4), 2026–2050. A further 8.2–9.0 Mt is committed after 2050 (later B2/B4 and C1–C4; outputs/reports/reconciliation.md). How fast existing dwellings are replaced is the largest structural uncertainty: Low replacement (the long-run rate throughout) gives 83.2 million m², High replacement (the 2018–2023 rate persisting) 98.7 million m². Within the Reference, joint uncertainty in the inputs gives a 90% interval of 69.1–109.9 million m² (median 88.9, mean 89.1). Outside the Monte Carlo, carbon-factor and soil bounds on the Reference carbon (21,578 kt): case-study jackknife 20,791–22,297 kt, single case study 17,043–25,846 kt, soil order 19,922–28,584 kt. Population uncertainty alone (Stats NZ 5th–95th percentiles) spans 66.7–112.3 million m². The joint interval is narrower than the population-only range because each population draw also moves household size along the matching Stats NZ Low/High variant: low-population variants come with smaller households (an older age structure), so the number of households varies less than population, whereas the population-only range holds household size on the Medium shape.

#### The 2026 overbuild rule

2026 building is observed, not modelled: 38,863 dwellings = 0.95 x consents over the latest 12 observed months (the year to July 2026; to be replaced by calendar 2026 when published). It exceeds the 2026 requirement by +16,760. From 2027 building stays above the requirement by gap_ref x rho^(t-2026), with gap_ref = building 2026 - requirement 2027 = +9,974 and rho = 0.52 (the estimated persistence of departures from the calibrated identity). The 2027 requirement is used because the 2026 requirement is depressed by the one-off 2026 population shortfall. The 2026 overbuild is STOCK-ADDING: the extra dwellings join the stock as additional vacant dwellings that are not absorbed (no payback), soil carbon loss applies (new footprints) and removals stay on the path of the replacement variant; +27,479 dwellings over 2026–2050, on top of whichever replacement variant runs. Implied stock vacancy (1 - households / (stock + cumulative 2026 overbuild)) peaks at 6.52% in 2031 and is 6.36% in 2050, against 5.08–8.09% at the censuses 1986–2023 (pre-2013 values on the earlier empty definition).

The vacancy-rate parameter is held at its published 2023 census value (5.39%; on the consistent definition 2023 is the series maximum, 5.38%, minimum 4.01% in 1996); implied stock vacancy rises to ≈6.4% because the 2026 overbuild is not absorbed. In 2050 implied stock vacancy is 1.0 percentage point above the 2023 rate; with payback (absorption 0.20 a year) floor area is -4.1%.

Caveats: a permanent 2026 overbuild assumes the extra vacant dwellings are never absorbed; over 2018–2023 part of the excess building went to redevelopment and household formation instead. rho is estimated on the calibrated identity, not on market cycles. Sensitivities: booking as stock-neutral redevelopment (implied net removals then peak at 23,041 in 2026), payback (absorption 0.20 or 0.10 a year), and the gap measured against the 2026 requirement.

#### Soil method

Soil carbon loss is the loss of soil organic carbon when land is built on (land-use change): a new building footprint seals the soil under it, while a rebuilt footprint sits on soil already sealed. Soil carbon loss is therefore applied to all floor area except the Replacement band (demolition, net of unconsented additions) and the Redevelopment band, where it is zero. The factor is 58.77 kg CO₂e per m² of footprint, the area-weighted average over the 10 soil orders of the land zoned for urbanisation to about 2050 in Auckland, divided by each typology's floor space index (Christoforatos, Pickering & Schipper 2026, Journal of Environmental Management 415, 130603, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jenvman.2026.130603). The Raw and Organic soil-order extremes are the bounding sensitivity. Carbon factors for materials come from 16 New Zealand case studies (Christoforatos & Pickering 2025, Smart and Sustainable Built Environment, https://doi.org/10.1108/SASBE-06-2025-0304).

### Validation

Rolling-origin hindcast of dwellings built (actual households and vacancy fed in; the net-replacement term predicted). Vacancy on a consistent definition (the pooled 2018/2023 empty share, 49.2% of unoccupied, at every census; the 2013 census share was 76.2%, and published empty vacancy falls 8.09% -> 5.08% across the 2013->2018 definitional break); vacancy as published in the last column.

| origin | test years | long-run rate (Low replacement rule) error | Reference rule error | best alternative | Reference rule, vacancy as published |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2006 | 2007–2023 | -7.1% | -6.1% | constant -0.4% | -16.2% |
| 2013 | 2014–2023 | -4.4% | -2.0% | constant -0.8% | -18.0% |
| 2018 | 2019–2023 | -14.7% | -10.5% | linked -8.5% | -10.5% |

Under a consistent vacancy definition the Reference rule reproduces building from the 2006 and 2013 origins to 2023 within 2–6%; the residual miss (-10.5% from 2018) is the 2018–23 surge.

2026 check (model run without any observed-2026 input): observed consents Jan-Jul 23,916 vs model 17,389; ratio 1.38.
Decomposition of the 2026 gap in the Reference (Jan-Jul 2026 / seasonal share): +11,049 dwellings = population -6,157 + pipeline from 2025 +0 + 2026 consents above requirement +17,206.

### Finding: 2026 building runs well above the model's requirement

Consents for January-July 2026 (23,916) are 1.38 times what the Reference, run without any 2026 data, implies for those months. In completions, observed-implied 2026 building is 40,482 dwellings against a Reference requirement of 29,434 (gap +11,049)[^low]. Population does not explain it: population growth over the year to June 2026 fell short of the projection, which lowers the requirement by 6,157. The gap is building already in the pipeline from 2025 (+0) plus 2026 consents above requirement (+17,206). Over 2018–2023 most building above household formation went to redevelopment (net removals 30,207) rather than vacancy (+6,286).

The model takes 2026 building from the observed consents and carries the excess forward as the 2026 overbuild (+16,760 dwellings in 2026, then gap_ref +9,974 fading at rho = 0.52; +27,479 dwellings over 2026–2050).

[^low]: In Low replacement (long-run rate) the requirement is 27,574 and the gap +12,908 = population -6,157 + pipeline +0 + 2026 consents above requirement +19,066.

### Planetary-boundary layer (AESA): climate change

Against the 2 °C carrying capacity (Bjørn & Hauschild 2015), allocated to the sector by acquired rights (AR; Horup et al. 2025) and ability to pay (AtP; Hjalsted et al. 2021), the boundary is 173.4 kt CO₂e (AR) and 43.35 kt (AtP) in 2026, and 183.5 / 45.87 kt in 2050 (AtP = 25.0% of AR in every year). Over 2026–2050 the Reference exceeds them 4.85-fold (AR; Monte Carlo p5-p95 3.90–5.75) and 19.4-fold (AtP; 15.5–23.1). The two principles are a range and are not averaged. Methods, constants, sources and limitations: the AESA section of outputs/reports/METHODS_DRAFT.md; settings: outputs/reports/ASSUMPTIONS.md. The emissions committed after 2050 (later B2/B4 and C1–C4) by the 2026–2050 cohorts (8,208–8,969 kt) equal 45–49 years of the 2050 AR boundary; they fall after 2050 and are not part of the cumulative LoE 2026–2050.

|---|---|
| DATA | Population: Stats NZ 2024-base projection percentiles; observed 2026 growth (DPE ERP) |
| DATA | Household-size shape: Stats NZ 2018-base household projections, rebased on observed households |
| DATA | Long-run net replacement: census private-dwelling counts and consents, 1991–2023 |
| DATA | 2026 building: 0.95 x consents over the latest 12 observed months (dwellings and floor area; the observed 2026 typology mix weights the case-study factors inside the model) |
| DATA | Typology mix (internal to the model): the 2022–2026 consented average |
| DATA | Dwelling size: consents 2023–2025; vacancy-rate parameter: the published 2023 census value |
| LITERATURE | Completion rate 0.95 (Jones et al. 2024; citation to verify) |
| LITERATURE | Demolition split 0.135%/yr (BRANZ SR214); total net replacement from census counts |
| LITERATURE | Material carbon factors: 16 NZ case studies (Christoforatos & Pickering 2025) |
| LITERATURE | Soil carbon loss 58.77 kg CO₂e/m² footprint, zero on the Replacement and Redevelopment bands (Christoforatos, Pickering & Schipper 2026) |
| JUDGEMENT | Replacement: in the Reference net replacement fades from the 2018–2023 rate to the long-run rate with half-life 10 yr; Low replacement and High replacement bound it |
| JUDGEMENT | 2026 overbuild: stock-adding (vacant dwellings), never absorbed, fading at rho |
| DECISION | Typology mix held in every variant (Low replacement, Reference, High replacement); internal to the model (it weights the case-study factors) and not reported |
| JUDGEMENT | Household size: interpolation through all published Stats NZ values (2018–2043), held constant beyond 2043 with zero slope imposed at 2043 |
| JUDGEMENT | No completion lag (same-year consents x 0.95) |

### Open limitations and data needs

- No national demolition data: demolition of detached buildings up to three storeys is consent-exempt, so the implied replacement rates cannot be tested against a count.
- N4 (open): the Low/High household-size variants (deterministic) are paired with stochastic population percentiles through one draw z, and the total vs private-household population question is unresolved until the living-arrangement table (E2); the household projections are 2018-base, with Stats NZ's 2023-base release (late 2026) to be adopted in a later version.
- Timber end of life (C1–C4) excludes biogenic CO2 (confirmed by the author). Whether it includes landfill methane is TO CONFIRM from Christoforatos & Pickering 2025 (author check).
- With the typology mix held in every variant (internal to the model: it weights the case-study factors), neither the variants nor the Monte Carlo carry typology-mix uncertainty; a change of mix is a pathway question for later work, not a baseline uncertainty.
- The soil factor was derived for Auckland's future urban zones and is applied nationally.
- The case-study carbon factor for apartments rests on one independent case study (A_1 and A_2 are one design at two scales).
- The regional analysis of redevelopment (replacement half-life by territorial authority) is deferred.
- Net replacement persistence (the replacement half-life of the Reference) is not identifiable from the census record; Low replacement and High replacement bound it.
- The 2018 census empty-dwelling count has no quality rating (DataInfo+); the vacancy terms rely on it.
- The 2026 overbuild fades at the persistence estimated on the calibrated stock identity (rho), not on market cycles (an assumption).
- W from Little's law is a lower bound on the completion lag.
- Retirement-village floor area is reported but out of carbon scope.
- The vacancy-rate parameter is held at its published 2023 census value (5.39%; on the consistent definition 2023 is the series maximum, 5.38%, minimum 4.01% in 1996); implied stock vacancy rises to ≈6.4% because the 2026 overbuild is not absorbed. The 2026 overbuild (≈27,500 dwellings over 2026–2050, of which ≈24,600 in 2026–2028) is not absorbed by later demand, so the implied stock vacancy stays about 1 percentage point above the 1986–2023 range on a consistent definition (4.0–5.4%). Absorption is not modelled: the persistence rho = 0.52 (lag-1 autocorrelation of the annual departure of building from the calibrated stock identity, 1992–2023) describes how a flow deviation fades (already used for the excess), not a payback of the stock, and the eight census vacancy observations do not identify a mean-reversion rate.
- Decarbonisation paths are relative changes for European and global market processes modelled with premise on ecoinvent 3.9.1 (Horup et al. 2025); they are applied as relative changes to New Zealand case-study factors. This assumes NZ material supply decarbonises at the same relative rate as those markets, which is not tested.
- Items without a counterpart in Horup et al. follow a labelled proxy path (polymers, paint and SIP at EPS, the smallest reduction in the set; gypsum plasterboard at clay brick) or are held at 2025 (the lift); the proxies are a judgement, bracketed by holding them at 2025 (sensitivity).
- C1–C4 (end of life) is held at 2025 factors (no source for end-of-life decarbonisation); future end-of-life technology would lower the committed emissions (conservative).
- Horup et al. (2025) SI Table S4 gives the average of the 9 premise scenarios only; the scenario range is shown graphically in their Fig. 2, so no low/high decarbonisation path is implemented.
- Several items are made in New Zealand with electricity-intensive production (aluminium, Pink Batts glass wool, Pacific Steel rebar, WPMA Radiata timber, Nelson Pine LVL); the aluminium items are stated in their EPD names to use mainly renewables-generated electricity. Where their 2025 factors already reflect low-carbon electricity, the premise paths, which include the decarbonisation of electricity supply ("The Premise software accounts for future changes in several critical sectors (supply of conventional and alternative fuels, electricity, cement and steel production and freight and passenger road transportation), and includes implementation of technologies such as carbon capture and storage in steel and cement production" (Horup et al. 2025, p. 5)), may overstate their relative reduction; a sensitivity holds them at 2025.
- Composite floor decking (an RC item containing its steel deck and rebar) follows the concrete-structure path because the source gives no split; this is conservative versus steel profile for the steel share.
- Event timing is deterministic (n events evenly spaced in the building life). Resch et al. (2021, Section 2.2 and Fig. 4) model replacement years as probability-distributed; the L / n sensitivity brackets the timing within the service-life range implied by the counts, but not early or late failures.
- A4–A5 follows a generic technological-progress factor (Resch et al. 2021, Table 1) because it cannot be separated by material process; Horup et al. (2025, Fig. 2A, pp. 5–6) show that generic factors oversimplify material-specific trends, and Resch et al. state that "the decay functions should not be interpreted as predictions" (p. 4). Sensitivities: held at 2025 and the item S4 paths.
- Emissions committed after 2050 (later B2/B4 and C1–C4) are a range bounded by two conventions (2025 factors; the 2050 factors held), not a projection: the source paths end in 2050 and C1–C4 has no decarbonisation source.
- The repaint composition differs from the first coat but cannot be separated in the source file; repaints take the line's initial stage split (negligible: the paint path is the EPS proxy).
- Completion rate 0.95: "Jones et al. 2024" is a citation to verify (TODO: confirm the reference before submission).

### Figures

The figures of the paper: outputs/headline/HEADLINE.md; every other figure: outputs/diagnostics/DIAGNOSTICS.md. Where the projection leaves the 1991–2025 range: outputs/reports/reality_checks.md.

## 2. Planetary-boundary layer (AESA)

The planetary-boundary layer is an absolute environmental sustainability assessment (AESA) of New Zealand new residential construction, climate change only, 2026–2050. Static carrying capacity; two allocation principles reported as a range and never averaged. This layer does not change the model; it reads the model's outputs.

### Equations as implemented (aesa.py)

**Acquired rights** (Horup et al. 2025, Sci. Total Environ. 966, 178780, Eq. 1, p. 4):

    B_AR(t) = SOS · (Ī_sec,base / I_glob) · [P_NZ(t) / P_NZ(t0)] · [P_W(t0) / P_W(t)],   t0 = 2025

Ī_sec,base is the mean annual sector impact 2016–2025 from this model's own history (same scope, accounting rule and soil convention as the projection; at 2025 case-study factors: past construction used past technology, so the decarbonisation of A1–A3 applies only to 2026–2050). Over the base window LoE_AR = I_glob / SOS = 8.1938 by construction (the sector impact cancels); the information is in the trajectory relative to the base.

**Ability to pay** (Hjalsted et al. 2021, J. Ind. Ecol. 25, 6–19, Table 2 Eqs. 5–6, p. 11; SI Eq. S1):

    SoSOS_ind(t) = SOS / P_W(t) · (g_W / g_NZ) · α
    B_AtP(t)     = SoSOS_ind(t) · P_NZ(t) · s_sec
    α            = 1 / Σ_c [(P_c / P_W) (g_W / g_c)]   (SI Eq. S1 with GDP totals, rewritten per capita)

g = GDP per capita in base year b = 2024, held fixed; g_W = Σ P_c g_c / Σ P_c and P_W = Σ P_c over the same covered economies. B_AtP / B_AR = (g_W/g_NZ) · α · s_sec · (P_NZ(t0)/P_W(t0)) · (I_glob/Ī_sec,base) is constant in this static design: 0.2500.

**Carbon factors.** A1–A3 of each case-study EPD item decarbonised 2026–2050 after Horup et al. (2025) SI Table S4 (item-level mapping, data/material_item_map.csv: direct, Horup p. 6, proxy or held), for construction and for the A1–A3 share of maintenance (B2, B4; replacement and repaint events); A4–A5 e^(-0.01 (t - 2025)) after Resch et al. (2021) Table 1; C1–C4, held items and soil carbon loss at 2025 (see outputs/reports/ASSUMPTIONS.md).

**Accounting.** Time-resolved: the sector impact I_sec(t) counts the materials and construction (A1–A5) and soil carbon loss of the construction in year t and the maintenance (B2, B4; replacement and repaint events) that occurs in year t in buildings built from 2026. Maintenance events after 2050 and all end-of-life emissions (C1–C4) of the 2026–2050 cohorts are committed after 2050, reported below as a range and in years of the 2050 AR boundary; they are not part of the cumulative LoE.

**Level of exceedance**: LoE_k(t) = I_sec(t) / B_k(t); cumulative LoE = Σ I_sec / Σ B_k over 2026–2050 (ratio of sums).

**Dating.** Model year t is 31 December (Stats NZ ERP history). The WPP 2024 series (1 July) and, in the sensitivities, the Stats NZ (30 June) and WPP New Zealand series are dated at t as the mean of mid-year t and t+1.

### Results

The 2 °C carrying capacity (Bjørn & Hauschild 2015) allocated by acquired rights gives 173.4 kt CO₂e in 2026 and 183.5 kt in 2050; by ability to pay 43.35 and 45.87 kt (25.0% of AR in every year). Both rise: New Zealand's share of world population grows between 2026 and 2050. Over 2026–2050 the Reference emits 21,578 kt against cumulative boundaries of 4,451 kt (AR) and 1,113 kt (AtP): cumulative LoE 4.85 (AR; Monte Carlo p5-p95 3.90–5.75) and 19.4 (AtP; 15.5–23.1).

### Limitations

- Static carrying capacity: the carrying capacities are constant yearly values modelled at steady state and their timespan may not match the assessment period (Clausen et al. 2025, pp. 143 and 148).
- Accounting (time-resolved): the sector impact of 2026–2050 counts materials and construction (A1–A5) and soil carbon loss in the construction year and maintenance (B2, B4) in the year it occurs. Maintenance after 2050 and all end-of-life emissions (C1–C4) of the 2026–2050 cohorts are committed after 2050, outside 2026–2050; they are reported as a range (outputs/data/aesa/results.json "committed", H6) in years of the 2050 AR boundary and are not compared with the 2026–2050 boundary. Whole life at construction is a sensitivity.
- History at 2025 factors: the acquired-rights base (2016–2025) and the base-window sensitivities use the 2025 case-study factors because no historical factor series exists for the case studies. If past production was more carbon-intensive than in 2025 (as the ~1%/yr technological progress assumed by Resch et al. 2021 implies), the base and hence the AR boundary are understated and the AR exceedance overstated (conservative); the size of this effect is not quantified. The base follows the projection's accounting rule (materials and construction and soil carbon loss of the base window's construction plus the maintenance within the base window of the cohorts built in it).
- The primary SOS (6.81E12) is the 2 °C carrying capacity of Bjørn & Hauschild (2015), not the 1 W/m² planetary boundary (3.61E12, sensitivity C). Sala et al. (2020, Table 3) label 6.81E12 as radiative forcing after Rockström et al. (2009), which does not match its derivation in Bjørn & Hauschild (2015).
- GWP basis: Bjørn & Hauschild (2015) ESM2 uses AR5 GWP100 factors (CH4 28, N2O 265; column "CFs (GWP100, IPCC5)") while their Table 1 cites Forster et al. (2007), i.e. AR4. The GWP basis of the case-study LCA factors used by the model is not documented in this repository (building_data.xlsx gives "GWP" columns only; source Christoforatos & Pickering 2025): to be confirmed by the author.
- I_glob = 5.58E13 (Bjørn & Hauschild 2015 ESM2, from Laurent et al. 2013, year 2010): Laurent et al. (2013) is not in hand, so whether it includes land-use-change CO2 (the sector impact includes soil carbon loss) and its GWP basis are NOT VERIFIED. The per-gas indicator scores in ESM2 sum to 54.0 Gt CO2-eq with 39.5 Gt CO2; a CO2 total of that size is consistent with inclusion of land-use-change CO2 (inference, not a sourced statement). The EC-JRC table "Normalization factors for testing" (Benini, Sala & Pant, version 0.1.1, 15 Dec 2015; sheet 1.3) gives the PROSUITE global value as 5.589E13 kg CO2-eq, 8,100 kg/person, "2010 or 2000".
- Final-consumption-expenditure upscaling: the numerator (consented residential value) is an investment flow (gross fixed capital formation), while Hjalsted et al. (2021) define the upscaling on final consumption and leave intermediate sectors as open (p. 16).
- Ability to pay: Hjalsted et al. (2021) state GDP as "USD/cap (2017)", World Bank (2019), without naming the series; current US$ is the sensitivity. The GDP coverage excludes economies without the measure (listed in outputs/data/aesa/results.json).
- Monte Carlo: I_sec,base is recomputed in every draw with that draw's case-study carbon factors (2025 technology), so the factor uncertainty is treated alike in the base and the projection; it does not co-vary with the draw's completion rate or dwelling size (historical floor area is observed).
- The numerical results in Hjalsted et al.'s SI (Tables S4-S9) are reproduced only with α = 1; we apply α as specified in their Eq. 5 and SI Eq. S1, which ensures national shares sum to the global SOS. The authors have been contacted.

### Notes

- The manuscript world population 2025 (8,231,613,070) equals the WPP 2024 Median sheet x 1000; its 2026–2028 values differ from it by +/-0.5 person, consistent with a source at a higher precision than the 3-decimal thousands in this file; they are not a dating convention (the mean of 1 July t and t+1 differs by ~34 M).
- In the Monte Carlo the AR boundary varies with each draw's NZ population path and with I_sec,base recomputed from the draw's case-study carbon factors (2025 technology) on the observed history; the AtP boundary varies with population only. mc_base_fixed gives the bands with I_sec,base held at its deterministic value.

## 3. Pathways and the theoretical limit

Five pathways for new residential construction in New Zealand, 2026–2050, built from five levers and applied to the Reference projection, assessed against the climate-change budgets of the planetary-boundary layer (AESA; acquired rights, AR; ability to pay, AtP). The model is unchanged: `pathways.py` re-calls `engine.forward()` with copies of the Reference inputs modified by `levers.py` (hooks: docs/HOOKS.md); no projection output is rewritten. With every lever off the run reproduces the Reference (maximum relative difference 4.4e-16; tests/test_pathways.py). Table 1: outputs/reports/LEVERS_TABLE.md.

### Pathways and demand bands

| pathway | levers | demand band targeted |
|---|---|---|
| P1 Right-sized dwellings | L1 Dwelling size | Extra space (and the dwelling size of every band except Population growth) |
| P2 Occupied stock | L2 Vacancy rate, L3 Overbuild absorption | Vacancy (including the change in the vacancy rate); 2026 overbuild |
| P3 Retained stock | L4 Building retention | Replacement and Redevelopment |
| P4 Low-carbon materials | L5 Material carbon | None: carbon per m² (A1–A3) of every band |
| P5 Combined | all five | all of the above |

**Typology mix.** The denser typology mix (lever of pathways_v2, removed in pathways_v3.1) was not carried forward: within the embodied-carbon scope a denser mix raises A1–A3 per m² (attached typologies carry more per m²), while its benefits (infrastructure, operational energy, land) are outside the scope. Values from git tag pathways_v2 (Reference): Moderate / Ambitious carbon -0.39% / -2.94% vs the Reference while carbon per m² rose from 240.9 to 241.9 / 248.8 kg CO₂e; its lever Shapley share was 1.7% / 5.8%. The typology shares stay at the Reference held mix in every run (the Reference, P1-P5 and TL).

Population growth and Smaller households are untargeted by design: population and household formation are exogenous (as in Pellan et al. 2024). Every run reports floor area and carbon by demand band (outputs/data/pathways/bands.csv), so the attribution by band is exact and needs no decomposition.

### Conventions

* Adoption path (all levers): s(y) = 1 / (1 + exp(−k (y − 2030.5))), k = ln(81)/6 = 0.7324 (s rises from 10% to 90% within 6 years); w(y) = (s(y) − s(2026)) / (s(2035) − s(2026)) for 2026 ≤ y ≤ 2035, w = 1 after 2035, w(2026) = 0: full roll-out by 2035 (adopted). A lever moves a quantity from its Reference value b to its target x as b + w(y)(x − b). Basis: full roll-out by 2035 following RECC (Pauliuk et al. 2024, J. Ind. Ecol. 28, 1699: circular-economy strategies fully implemented by 2035). Sensitivities (P5), same k: full roll-out by 2030 (midpoint 2028.5, full strength 2030) and by 2045 (midpoint 2035.5, full strength 2045; the same adoption speed ten years later).
* 2026 is observed (consented floor area fixed) and identical in every run.
* 2026 overbuild: held at the Reference path, in dwellings, except where L3 absorbs it (it is the observed 2026 pipeline, not demand).
* Accounting as the Reference (time-resolved): carbon 2026–2050 = materials and construction (A1–A5) and soil carbon loss in the construction year + maintenance (B2, B4), 2026–2050; later B2/B4 events and all C1–C4 of the 2026–2050 cohorts are committed after 2050 (range: lower with the 2050 factors held, upper at 2025 factors; `events.committed` with each run's floor area by typology).

### Levers as implemented (levers.py)

    L1   size_t(y) = occ_t(y) + [1 − f w(y)] (size_ref_t − occ_t(y)),   occ_t(y) = S(y) · OLF_t
    L2   v(y) = v0 + w(y)(v* − v0)
    L3   join = market_excess(E_nojoin, O26, ρ, 2027, surplus, absorption a)
    L4   demol(y) = demol · (1 − w(y) d);  resid(y) = resid_LR + (resid_REF(y) − resid_LR)(1 − w(y) d)
    L5   A1-A3_t(y) = [1 − w(y)(1 − r)] · (A1-A3_t,2025 − R13_t(y))   (A4–A5, B events, C1–C4, soil unchanged)

S and OLF are the engine's (S = population / households of the median path; OLF per typology from the case studies), so occ_t is the occupied area the engine uses for the population-growth and extra-space bands. size_ref: realised new-dwelling size, mean of 2023–2025. L1 removes a share f of the extra-space margin (size − S(y) · OLF): full strength in 2035, f held constant to 2050, so the sizes then follow S(y). L1 holds a typology / year at size_ref where size_ref ≤ occ (never binds: 0 typology-years held). L2 acts through the stock identity: while v falls the vacancy-change term releases existing dwellings once (cumulative release in outputs/data/pathways/runs.csv, by year in outputs/data/pathways/annual.csv); under the logistic adoption path the release peaks where w rises fastest (2029–2032). R13: the A1–A3 decarbonisation of the Reference (Horup et al. 2025, item level).

#### L5: Harrell-Davis estimator

Sample: the 14 independent case studies of the detached and townhouse typologies (duplicates excluded; apartments have one independent case and are not in the sample), 2025 A1–A3 per m² (outputs/data/factors/factors_building.csv). Scale-free ratio x_i = A1-A3_i / pooled A1–A3 of its typology (pooling as Building_factors.pool; recomputed pooled values equal the model's to 2.8e-14 kg/m²). Harrell & Davis (1982):

    Q̂(q) = Σ_i W_i x_(i),   W_i = I_{i/n}(a, b) − I_{(i−1)/n}(a, b),   a = q(n + 1),   b = (1 − q)(n + 1)

with I the regularised incomplete beta function, implemented directly and checked against scipy.stats.mstats.hdquantiles (≤ 1e-10). Interval: nonparametric bootstrap of the cases, B = 10,000, seed 20261008, percentile 95% (Efron & Tibshirani 1993). The pathway runs use the point estimate; the same r applies to all three typologies (apartments held at r = 1 as a sensitivity).

### Attribution

Shapley values (Shapley 1953; for emissions decompositions Albrecht, François & Schoors 2002) of each player for the reduction v(∅) − v(N):

    φ_i = Σ_{S ⊆ N∖{i}} |S|! (|N| − |S| − 1)! / |N|! · [v(S) − v(S ∪ {i})]

Players: the four pathways P1-P4 (|N| = 4, 16 subsets; main) and the five levers (|N| = 5, 32 subsets; SI); every subset is a full run; v = cumulative carbon 2026–2050 (kt) or cumulative LoE AR. Computed in exact rational arithmetic on the run values, so Σ_i φ_i = Reference − P5 exactly (tested).

### AESA gap

Budgets B_AR(t), B_AtP(t) for the Reference from outputs/data/aesa/annual.csv (no lever changes population). Cumulative LoE = Σ I(t) / Σ B(t) over 2026–2050 (aesa.cumulative_loe); remaining reduction needed = 1 − 1/LoE.

**Back-cast.** I(t; k) = F(t) + k · G(t), F the 2026 cohort (its materials and construction (A1–A5), soil carbon loss and maintenance (B2, B4), 2026–2050), G the 2027–2050 cohorts; scaling their floor area by k keeps the typology mix and the replacement share, hence the soil share. k solves Σ I(t; k) = Σ B_AR(t) (scipy.optimize.brentq on [0, 1], xtol 1e-15; checked against the closed form). AtP: the minimum attainable cumulative LoE is Σ F / Σ B_AtP (k = 0).

**Solution space** (after Horup et al. 2025, Fig. 6): I(t; d, i) = F(t) + (1 − d)[(1 − i) G_ns(t) + G_soil(t)] on the Reference. Pathways sit at d = 1 − floor area_P / floor area_REF and i = 1 − (C_P / floor area_P) / (C_REF / floor area_REF) (2027–2050 cohorts; C = their materials and construction (A1–A5) and maintenance (B2, B4), 2026–2050, without soil carbon loss); a negative i would mean more carbon per m².

### Checks (tests/test_pathways.py, tests/test_regression_model_v1.py)

* No lever = the Reference (≤ 1e-9 relative): annual carbon, materials and construction (A1–A5) with soil carbon loss, maintenance (B2, B4) 2026–2050, floor area by typology, demand bands, committed range, cumulative LoE AR / AtP; Low replacement and High replacement without levers = their runs in the planetary-boundary layer (AESA).
* Each lever at zero strength = the Reference; 2026 identical in every run; lever functions never modify their inputs; the logistic adoption path is 0 in 2026, 1 from 2035 and monotone.
* L1 sizes ≥ occupied area S·OLF in every typology, year and run; D ≥ S·OLF (engine extra_clip = 0); implied vacancy ≥ 4.0%; no negative dwellings built.
* Harrell-Davis = scipy.stats.mstats.hdquantiles (≤ 1e-10); pathway and lever Shapley efficiency exact; demand bands add up to the totals; back-cast LoE AR = 1 (≤ 1e-9).
* Numerical lock (tests/test_regression_model_v1.py): every number the model reported before the renaming and restructuring of this release (captured in tests/regression_model_v1.json) is reproduced at its release location to 1e-12 relative.

### Limitations

* L4 is an upper bound: the carbon of renovating the buildings kept in use is not modelled (Napiontek et al. 2025, Resour. Conserv. Recycl. 215, 108117).
* L5 rests on 14 case studies; the Ambitious interval is wide (0.61–0.95). The ratio is pooled across detached and townhouses (scale-free) and applied to apartments too (one independent apartment case; held at r = 1 as a sensitivity), and to the pooled A1–A3 of every item: the best-practice material mix is assumed transferable.
* L1 keeps the engine's occupied area (S·OLF) and cuts only the space above it; the occupancy load factor per typology and design rules (minimum room sizes) are not modelled.
* The typology mix is held at the Reference (the denser mix removed; see above): the infrastructure, operational-energy and land benefits of denser forms are outside the embodied-carbon scope.
* L2 starts from the Reference, in which the vacancy-rate parameter is held at its published 2023 census value (5.39%; on the consistent definition 2023 is the series maximum, 5.38%, minimum 4.01% in 1996); implied stock vacancy rises to ≈6.4% because the 2026 overbuild is not absorbed. v0 = 5.39% is the published 2023 empty-dwelling share while the target range (4.01% in 1996 to 5.38% in 2023) is on a consistent definition; targets rounded to 0.1 point; 4.0% is the lowest NZ vacancy rate on that definition. The release of existing dwellings acts once, while the rate falls.
* The 2026 overbuild is held in dwellings, so its floor area follows L1 through the blended size.
* Levers are parameter changes on the Reference model; no behavioural, market or rebound response is modelled; interactions are those of the model (attributed by Shapley values).
* The pathways are deterministic (median demographics); the Monte Carlo is not re-run for them. Budgets are static (the limitations of the planetary-boundary layer (AESA) apply).
* Omitted: Occupancy / household size (household size is a demographic input of the projection (Stats NZ household projections, projection.HH_SIZE_VARIANT) and sets the number of households, not a construction choice; a lever on it needs a behavioural or policy model of household formation that the model does not have (Population growth and Smaller households are untargeted by design, as in Pellan et al. 2024)); Brownfield soil (the soil factor is one area-weighted value for Auckland land zoned for urbanisation (Christoforatos, Pickering & Schipper 2026) and soil carbon loss is already zero on the replacement bands; no national brownfield share is in the inputs to parameterise a shift (TL6 Urban infill bounds it in the theoretical limit)); Lightweighting (the case studies give A1–A3 per m² by material and item, not structural mass by design alternative; a mass reduction cannot be separated from the material choice already covered by L5); Bio-based archetypes (no typology has a bio-based archetype among the 16 case studies, and the model's biogenic-carbon convention (timber C1–C4 excludes biogenic CO2) would need extending; overlaps L5).


### Theoretical limit TL

> TL is a hyper-optimistic theoretical limit; a thought experiment, not a pathway: all assumptions at full strength from 1 January 2027, combining best observed attributes of different buildings and places; not a proposal or a feasible pathway (potentials hierarchy: theoretical > technical > realisable).

**Definition.** TL = P5 Ambitious with six overrides at full strength from 1 January 2027 (w = 1 for every lever in 2027–2050, no adoption path; 2026 observed and untouched): TL1 No vacancy (v = 0; the 2026 overbuild absorbed in full), TL2 No extra space (new-dwelling size = occupied area S(t) · OLF), TL3 Minimum space per person (OLF of every new building = the lowest independent design OLF), TL4 Best-practice materials (each typology at its own best independent case; apartments held), TL5 Lowest-carbon soils (lowest soil order), TL6 Urban infill (a share s of the non-replacement new floor area on previously developed land, zero soil carbon loss). L4 (−40%) as P5 Ambitious; the typology shares stay at the Reference held mix. The adopted decarbonisation applies in TL as in every run (A1–A3 item paths of Horup et al. 2025, A4–A5 e^(-0.01 (t - 2025)); the lift held at 2025 as in the Reference). The potentials hierarchy (theoretical > technical > realisable) places TL at the theoretical end; TL, gradual adoption (SI) is a sensitivity.

| item | how it works (model terms) | assumption | TL value | source (full citation) | tag |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| TL1 No vacancy | v = 0 from 2027 (`v`); the 2026 overbuild absorbed in full; banking rule: built_t = max(0, raw_t - bank_(t-1)), unused release carried forward; stock-adding join = built - requirement | every vacant dwelling usable where needed, reallocated from 1 January 2027 | v = 0; absorption 1 | DECISION (author): theoretical limit of L2 / L3 | DECISION |
| TL2 No extra space | L1 with f = 1: size = occupied area S(t) x OLF (TL3's OLF) (`size`) | no space above the occupied area | f = 1 (2050 size 52.2 m² with TL3) | DECISION (author): theoretical limit of L1 | DECISION |
| TL3 Minimum space per person | OLF of every new building = the lowest design OLF (floor area / design occupants) of the independent case studies (`olf`, all typologies) | an apartment-block occupancy applied to every typology | 19.69 m²/person (A_1); replaces Detached 36.46, Townhouses 33.11, Apartments 20.63 | DATA: Christoforatos G, Pickering K (2025) Smart and Sustainable Built Environment, doi:10.1108/SASBE-06-2025-0304 (data/building_data.xlsx; duplicate A_2 excluded) | DATA |
| TL4 Best-practice materials | each typology's A1–A3 per m² at its own best independent case, on top of decarbonisation (as L5) | the best observed design of each typology built everywhere | Detached r = 0.530 (SD_2), Townhouses r = 0.880 (T_2), Apartments r = 1.000 (held: one independent case) | DATA: case studies (outputs/data/factors/factors_building.csv, 2025 factors) | DATA |
| TL5 Lowest-carbon soils | soil factor at the lowest soil order (SOC_low), applied exactly through the soil-bearing share | the lowest of 10 soil orders under every new footprint | Detached 22.9 (vs 50.1), Townhouses 13.8 (vs 30.3), Apartments 2.5 (vs 5.5) kg CO₂e/m² | DATA: Christoforatos G, Pickering K, Schipper LA (2026) Journal of Environmental Management 415, 130603 (the existing lower-bound sensitivity) | DATA |
| TL6 Urban infill | a share s of each year's non-replacement new floor area 2027–2050 is on previously developed land (zero soil carbon loss); the rest carries the TL5 factor: soil factor x (1 - s) on the soil-bearing floor area | (i) Auckland's observed share applied nationally (demonstrated-limit logic, as TL3 / TL4); (ii) a dwelling-count share applied to floor area; (iii) intensification on developed land seals no additional soil (upper bound: some infill builds over garden soil); (iv) replacement floor area keeps its existing zero-soil treatment; (v) the soil factor on the remaining share is TL5's lowest soil order | s = 0.82 x 0.79 = 0.648, rounded 0.65 | DATA: Auckland Council (2021). Auckland Plan 2050 Development Strategy Monitoring Report, December 2021: in 2020/21, 82% of dwelling consents were in the existing urban area, of which 79% occurred through intensification (Auckland monitoring); DECISION (author): national application | DATA + DECISION |

Table note: TL is a hyper-optimistic theoretical limit; a thought experiment, not a pathway: all assumptions at full strength from 1 January 2027, combining best observed attributes of different buildings and places; not a proposal or a feasible pathway (potentials hierarchy: theoretical > technical > realisable).

**Banking rule (TL1).** raw_t = requirement_t + absorbed 2026 overbuild_t (negative when the release of vacant or surplus dwellings exceeds the year's need); D_t = raw_t − bank_(t−1); built_t = max(0, D_t); bank_t = max(0, −D_t). The banked path enters engine.forward as a stock-adding join, join_t = built_t − requirement_t (join_redev = 0), so the stock identity holds and implied vacancy = stock_join / (households + stock_join) ≥ 0. Banked zero-building years carry floating-point noise of about 1e-12 dwellings; the checks use 1e-6 dwellings. The banking rule is applied in every TL-family run (it binds only where the release exceeds the need).

**Soil path (TL5, TL6).** The engine takes one soil factor per typology; the year-dependent factor is applied exactly by replacing the engine soil term in the intensity: I'(y) = I(y) − SOC_avg · share(y) + SOC_path(y) · share(y), with share(y) the soil-bearing (non-replacement) share of the floor area built in year y, taken from the engine and independent of the intensity (identical in both passes; tested). TL5: SOC_path = SOC_low. TL6: SOC_path(y) = SOC_TL5(y) · (1 − s w(y)), s = 0.82 × 0.79 = 0.648, rounded 0.65, i.e. a share s of each year's non-replacement floor area carries zero soil carbon loss and the rest the TL5 factor (tested to 1e-9). The engine share is 1 − soil-free / total floor area; in banked years with no new building (total ≈ 0, floating-point noise) it is undefined, so share(y) is clipped to [0, 1] and set to 0 where the floor area built is ≤ 1e-3 m² (a correction of the earlier version; CHANGELOG.md).

**TL6 source and assumptions.** Auckland Council (2021). Auckland Plan 2050 Development Strategy Monitoring Report, December 2021: in 2020/21, 82% of dwelling consents were in the existing urban area, of which 79% occurred through intensification. Assumptions: (i) Auckland's observed share applied nationally (demonstrated-limit logic, as TL3 / TL4); (ii) a dwelling-count share applied to floor area; (iii) intensification on developed land seals no additional soil (upper bound: some infill builds over garden soil); (iv) replacement floor area keeps its existing zero-soil treatment; (v) the soil factor on the remaining share is TL5's lowest soil order. Tag: DATA (the Auckland shares) + DECISION (author: their national application to floor area).

#### Limitations of TL

* TL combines attributes of different buildings and places (the OLF of A_1, an apartment block, applied to every typology; each typology's best A1–A3 case; the lowest soil order everywhere; Auckland's 2020/21 intensification share nationally) that have not been observed together; it is a hyper-optimistic thought experiment, not a design, a policy or a feasible pathway.
* TL2 + TL3 give every new dwelling the occupied area of the case-study minimum (about 20 m² per person); no design rule, accessibility standard or household-size variation is modelled.
* TL1 assumes every vacant dwelling is usable where it is needed (no spatial or condition mismatch; Napiontek et al. 2025 on hibernating stock) and an immediate reallocation in 2027.
* TL6 is an upper bound on the soil saving (assumption iii: some infill builds over garden soil) and transfers a dwelling-count share of one city to national floor area; its benefits beyond soil (infrastructure, transport energy) are outside the embodied-carbon scope, as for the removed denser typology mix.
* As in P1-P5, the renovation carbon of the retained stock (L4) and any rebound are not modelled; deterministic, median demographics; static budgets.
